jurisdiction.name: Texas
jurisdiction.notes: Texas has no state business license; the core state items are SOS entity formation, the Comptroller sales tax permit, TWC unemployment registration and, for alcohol, a TABC permit that cannot be filed until the city and county have certified the address as 'wet'. Retail food permits are issued by the local health department (Austin Public Health, Houston Health Department, etc.); Texas DSHS issues the retail food establishment permit ($258–$773 by gross food sales) only where no local health jurisdiction exists. Since July 1, 2026 mobile food vendors are licensed statewide by DSHS under HB 2844.

permits.name: Form your legal entity with the Texas Secretary of State (Form 205 LLC Certificate of Formation)
permits.issuing_agency: Texas Secretary of State – Business & Public Filings Division (SOSDirect)
permits.notes: File Form 205 (Certificate of Formation – Limited Liability Company) online through SOSDirect; the filing fee is $300 (a small card convenience fee applies online). You must name a registered agent with a Texas address who has consented to serve. Do this first: the EIN, Comptroller permit, lease, and every TABC application are issued to the entity name. A sole proprietor files an assumed name certificate with the county clerk instead.

permits.name: Texas Sales and Use Tax Permit
permits.notes: Free, but the Comptroller may require a security bond from some applicants; allow 2–3 weeks for the permit to arrive. Required for anyone selling taxable items, including prepared food and drinks. TABC's new-license checklist requires registration with the Comptroller before the alcohol application, so file this in week one. Mixed-drink sellers also owe the separate mixed beverage gross receipts and sales taxes, which are registered through the TABC permit.

permits.name: Register as an employer with the Texas Workforce Commission (unemployment tax)
permits.issuing_agency: Texas Workforce Commission (TWC) – Unemployment Tax Registration
permits.notes: Free online registration (about 20 minutes) that must be done within 10 days of becoming liable for state unemployment tax. A TWC tax account number is issued immediately; the Employer Liability Notice arrives by mail about two weeks later. Your payroll provider needs the account number before the first pay run.

permits.name: Workers' compensation coverage decision (optional in Texas) / non-subscriber notice
permits.issuing_agency: Texas Department of Insurance – Division of Workers' Compensation (DWC)
permits.notes: Texas is the only state where most private employers may opt out of workers' comp. If you buy a policy, premiums are a percentage of payroll, not a permit fee. If you opt out you become a 'non-subscriber': you must report non-coverage to DWC through the Employer E-File site, post notices to employees, report qualifying injuries, and you lose common-law defenses in injury lawsuits, so most restaurants buy coverage or an occupational injury plan. Landlords, event venues and some city permits ask for proof of coverage.

permits.name: TABC local certification (city secretary + county clerk wet/dry) and 60-day posting
permits.issuing_agency: City secretary / city clerk and county clerk where the premises is located (per TABC Form L-CERT)
permits.notes: Before TABC will accept an original retail application, the city secretary and the county clerk must each certify on Form L-CERT (or the AIMS summary) that the address is 'wet' for the permit type; by statute they have 30 days to certify or refuse. At a location not licensed for on-premise sales in the prior 24 months you must also post TABC's outdoor sign and keep it up for 60 days before TABC issues the permit, and mixed-beverage applicants publish notice in two consecutive newspaper issues. Start the sign and certification the week the lease is signed.
permits.stall_risk: A dry or partially dry precinct, or an address inside 300 ft of a church, school or hospital, means the clerk refuses to certify and the whole alcohol timeline stops. Ask the city and county clerk to pre-check the address before signing a lease.

permits.name: TABC Mixed Beverage Permit (MB) – spirits, wine and beer on-premise
permits.notes: Required for any bar or restaurant serving spirits. TABC's chart (fees effective 9/1/21) lists $5,300 for an original two-year MB permit ($2,650 renewal); cities and counties may each add a local fee of up to half the state fee, plus a conduct surety bond and newspaper notice. Older guidance quoting a separate state surcharge predates that chart. TABC quotes 30–35 days once the application is complete, but the 60-day sign posting sets the real minimum. MB holders also remit the 6.7% mixed beverage gross receipts tax plus mixed beverage sales tax, and at least one person named on the permit must take TABC's opioid overdose course.
permits.stall_risk: Incomplete AIMS applications are removed (fee refunded) if you miss TABC's 10-business-day deadline to answer an information request, which restarts the clock. Have the notarized ownership, lease and personal-history documents ready before filing and watch the AIMS inbox daily.

permits.name: TABC Food and Beverage Certificate (FB) – restaurant add-on to MB / BG / BE
permits.notes: A certificate filed alongside the MB, BG or BE permit (same AIMS application) for businesses that qualify as restaurants or keep alcohol at 60% or less of total sales. It is mandatory where the local-option election only allows mixed drinks in restaurants ('MB with FB required') and it unlocks exceptions such as on-premise sales near day-care centers. Two-year TABC fee $1,100, plus any local fee.
permits.renewal: Every two years with the primary permit

permits.name: TABC Wine and Malt Beverage Retailer's Permit (BG) or Beer Retailer's On-Premise License (BE)
permits.notes: Beer-and-wine service uses the BG permit (wine and malt beverages, on- and off-premise; two-year TABC fee $1,900). If you will pour beer only, the cheaper BE Retail Dealer's On-Premise License ($1,100, requires adequate seating) is enough; pick one, not both. Add the FB certificate if you operate as a restaurant. Local city and county fees of up to half the state fee, a conduct surety bond (BG), and the 60-day sign apply as for MB.

permits.name: TABC Private Club Registration Permit (N) – members-only service in a dry area
permits.notes: Only relevant if the clerk certifies your address as dry for the permit you want: an N permit lets a nonprofit club entity store and serve spirits, wine and beer to members even in a dry area (two-year TABC fee $2,600). The club needs a membership structure (patrons join at the door) and usually a separate management agreement with the operating company. Austin and Houston are wet, so this item is shown only for other Texas cities; if your address certifies wet, use the MB or BG permit instead.

permits.name: TABC Late Hours Certificate (LH) – alcohol service midnight to 2 a.m.
permits.notes: Lets MB, BG, BE and N holders sell or serve between midnight and 2 a.m. where local option allows late hours (Austin and Houston do). Two-year TABC fee $1,100 plus local fees; file it with the original application rather than as a later change. Some cities, including Austin, also apply zoning rules to late-hours alcohol uses near residential property.

permits.name: TABC seller/server certification for staff (voluntary, safe-harbor protection)
permits.notes: Not required by state law, but it is what protects your permit: under the 'safe harbor' rule TABC will not take administrative action against the business for an employee's illegal sale if every server and their managers were certified within 30 days of hire, you have written responsible-service policies, and you did not encourage the violation. The course takes about two hours online and the certificate is valid two years. Many insurers price liquor liability on it.

permits.name: Certified Food Manager (one on duty) + Food Handler cards for all food employees
permits.issuing_agency: DSHS-licensed / ANSI-accredited exam and training providers (25 TAC §228.31, §228.33)
permits.notes: Texas Food Establishment Rules require a Certified Food Manager (passed an accredited exam such as ServSafe) on site during operating hours, except minimal-risk prepackaged-only operations, and every other food employee must complete an accredited food handler course within 30 days of hire (statewide since 2016); handler cards are valid two years. Local health departments must accept any DSHS-approved certificate and will ask for the CFM at the pre-opening inspection. Where no local health department exists, DSHS itself issues the retail food permit ($258–$773 by annual food sales).

permits.name: Texas state Hotel Occupancy Tax registration (6%)
permits.notes: Hotels, motels, B&Bs and other lodging must collect the 6% state hotel occupancy tax on rooms of $15 or more per day and file with the Comptroller (a 1% discount applies for timely filing). Register when you apply for the sales tax permit. City and county hotel taxes are separate and are registered and paid to the local taxing authority, not the state.

permits.name: DSHS statewide Mobile Food Vendor license (food truck / trailer / cart)
permits.issuing_agency: Texas Department of State Health Services (DSHS) – Consumer Protection Division
permits.notes: Since July 1, 2026 (HB 2844) every mobile food vendor in Texas needs one DSHS license per vehicle, valid statewide; city health medallions in Austin and Houston no longer apply. Fees by risk tier, due at submission: Type I (no TCS food) $309; Type II (limited handling) $618 + $400 pre-licensing inspection; Type III (full cooking) $876 + $500. A new vendor cannot operate until the pre-licensing inspection is passed. Local fire inspections for propane and cooking equipment still happen at the city level.
permits.renewal: Annually, one year after the inspection is passed
